questions.question: How do constants and iota work in Go?
questions.title: Constants and iota in Go
questions.direct_answer: A Go constant is an immutable compile-time value. In a const block, iota starts at zero and increments for each constant specification, making it useful for enum-like values and bit flags.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know constants are compile-time values and can model a small enum safely.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting iota to persist across blocks or using an untyped constant where a runtime value is required.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that iota resets to zero in each const block and constants can remain untyped until context gives them a type.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Constants and iota in Go simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Compile-time named values
sections.content: Constants cannot be changed at runtime. `iota` is a counter scoped to one const declaration block.

sections.title: Enum-like constants
sections.content:
```go
type Level int
const (
  Low Level = iota
  Medium
  High
)
```

sections.title: Remember
items: iota begins at zero in each const block.
Constants are evaluated at compile time.
Use typed constants when APIs should reject unrelated values.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Constants are immutable compile-time values. I use iota inside a const block for enum-like sequences; it starts at zero, increments per specification, and resets in a new block.
